scope.flow: ServiceManager.registerAgents agent-instance registration for a service
evidence: Neither the `ServiceManager.registerAgents` nor `ServiceRegistry.registerAgents` functions check whether the given instances addresses are already in use as operator address. So if a malicious operator uses another operator's address as an instance address while registering agent instances for a service, it will permanently block the other operator from registering any agent instance for any service in the future.

An attacker can create a service with many slots just for this purpose. This attack cannot be stopped by pausing the `ServiceManager` as there is not pause check in the `ServiceManager.registerAgents` function.

The operator whitelist too is not helpful in this case as it is per service not global. So if the attacker creates his service, the whitelist won't help. The service can be created without the intention to push it to deploy but only to keep it at `ActiveRegistration` state just to be able to register instances and DOS other operators.

- Any operator can use any other operator's address as an instance address while registering agent instances for a service. This will permanently block the other operator from registering any agent instance for any service in the future, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS) attack.

Add a mapping in `ServiceManager` contract to keep track of all operator addresses so that it will be checked when calling `ServiceManager.registerAgents` if any of the provided instances address is already an operator address. At the end of the function (meaning registration successful), add the operator address to the mapping by mapping it with the number of registered instances. During `ServiceManager.unbond`, reduce the mapped number of registered instances so that when 0, the address can be used as an instance address later.

statements.text: An operator must be able to register instances for many services with the same address.
evidence: The DOS'ed operators can use another address but this will make managing instances harder for the operators. Plus the design supports registration of multiple/unlimited instances per operator for different services so this feature will be broken. Even worse, the malicious operator can keep registering any new operator address to ensure the DOS.
- The feature where an operator can register instances for many services with the same address is broken.

ambiguities: Report does not state whether the attacker must be a registered/whitelisted operator for the target service or how the attacker obtains authorization to register instances.
Report does not specify the exact state transition or prior transaction establishing the victim's operator registration beyond the general claim that operators use addresses to register instances.
The permanent-block outcome is described as a consequence of the missing collision check; the precise revert/error on the victim's later registration is not given.
Whether the attacker's service must be in ActiveRegistration at the moment of registration is implied but not stated as a strict precondition.
